analogy.p: Swing a ball round your head on a string. The ball's speed stays steady but its direction keeps changing, so it accelerates, and the string pulls it towards your hand (the centre). The string tension plays the role of gravity. If you swing it faster, the string must pull harder; for a fixed pull the only way to keep the circle is the right speed. The analogy breaks down because a string pulls with a force that you can adjust, whereas gravity gets weaker with distance and cannot be changed, and there is no string in space.
analogy.t: A ball on a string, swung in a circle

bullets: Gravity is the **force that holds an orbit together**; it acts towards the centre of the orbit.
A body in a circular orbit moves at **constant speed** but its **velocity is constantly changing** because its direction is constantly changing.
Because velocity is changing, the body is **accelerating**, even though its speed is constant.
A **stable orbit** has a particular speed for each radius. If speed changes, the radius must change.
**Natural satellites** are moons orbiting planets; **artificial satellites** are man-made objects orbiting a planet or moon.
Links: forces and motion (4.5), speed = distance / time, circumference of a circle, and space physics (4.8).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This point is about **orbital motion**. You need to know that **gravity** provides the force that allows planets and satellites, both **natural** (such as the Moon) and **artificial** (man-made), to stay in **circular orbits**. You must be able to explain, in words, that an object moving at a constant speed in a circle has a **changing velocity** and therefore is **accelerating**, and that the force making this happen points **towards the centre** of the circle. Finally, you need to explain that **for a stable orbit the radius must change if the speed changes**. These ideas are only tested qualitatively, but you still need the correct vocabulary.

bullets: **Natural satellite example:** the Moon orbiting the Earth; the large planets also have many moons.
**Artificial satellite examples:** communications, weather monitoring, navigation (GPS) and Earth observation satellites.
All of these are held in orbit by **gravity**; no engine is needed to keep a satellite going once it is in orbit at the right speed.
The Sun is the centre of the Solar system; the planets are held in their orbits by the Sun's gravity.
The satellite is **always falling towards** the planet but moves sideways fast enough that it keeps missing it, so it stays in orbit.
Different satellites orbit at different heights: low orbits for observation, higher orbits for others, but the same physics applies to all.
core.p: A **satellite** is any object that orbits a larger object in space. **Natural satellites** are moons such as our Moon, which orbits the Earth. **Artificial satellites** are made by people and launched into orbit around the Earth (or another body); they are used for communications, weather forecasting, navigation and observation. In both cases the satellite is kept in orbit by the **gravitational attraction** of the body it orbits. Planets themselves orbit the Sun because of the Sun's gravity.

bullets: Gravity always **attracts**; it is a **non-contact force**.
In a circular orbit, gravity acts **towards the centre** and the velocity is **along the tangent**: the two are at **90 degrees** to each other.
A force at right angles to the motion **changes direction but not speed**, which is why the orbit stays circular at constant speed.
The gravitational force on a satellite is weaker the further it is from the planet.
The term **centripetal force** means the resultant force pointing towards the centre of a circular path; in orbits it is provided by gravity.
Bigger mass of the central body means stronger gravity at a given distance.
core.h: Gravity as the force that provides the orbit
core.p: **Gravity** is an attractive, non-contact force between any two masses. The Earth pulls the Moon and satellites towards its centre, and the Sun pulls the planets towards its centre. This gravitational force acts at **right angles to the direction of travel** of the satellite, so it changes the **direction** of motion rather than the speed. The force always points to the centre of the orbit, so it is called the **centripetal force** for this motion. The strength of gravity gets **weaker as the distance from the centre increases**.

bullets: Velocity is a **vector** (size and direction); speed is a **scalar** (size only).
A change in **direction** is a change in velocity, so the body **accelerates**.
Acceleration is **towards the centre**, in the direction of the resultant force.
Typical wording: 'the **speed is constant but the direction is changing so the velocity is changing**, therefore it is **accelerating**'.
There is **no force along the direction of motion** that is needed to keep the speed constant in an orbit, because there is almost no air resistance in space.
This links to 4.5: resultant force causes acceleration (Newton's second law).
core.p: **Speed** is a scalar: it only has a size. **Velocity** is a **vector**: it has a size **and a direction**. A satellite in a circular orbit moves at constant speed, but its direction is always changing as it goes around, so its **velocity changes continuously**. Because **acceleration** is the rate of change of velocity, the satellite is **accelerating** all the time, even though it does not speed up or slow down. The acceleration points in the same direction as the resultant force, towards the centre of the circle.

bullets: For each **orbital radius** there is **one speed** that gives a stable circular orbit.
**Smaller radius = stronger gravity = higher orbital speed**; **larger radius = weaker gravity = lower orbital speed**.
If the speed changes, the satellite will move to a **new radius**; it can only stay in a stable orbit at the new radius if its speed matches that radius.
The Moon, which is far away, moves more slowly than a satellite orbiting close to the Earth.
Planets nearer the Sun (like Mercury) move faster in their orbits than planets further away (like Neptune), which also have much longer orbits.
Typical mark-scheme wording: 'for a stable orbit, if the speed changes the **radius** must change'.
Extension (not required): for a circular orbit, speed v = square root of (G x M / r), which shows that a larger r gives a smaller v.
core.h: Why the radius must change if the speed changes
core.p: At any given distance from the planet, gravity has a fixed strength, and a satellite on a **stable circular orbit** at that distance must move at one particular speed: the speed for which gravity provides exactly the force needed to keep it on that circle. If the satellite is moving **faster** than this, gravity is too weak to bend its path enough and the satellite moves into a **larger orbit**. If it moves **slower**, gravity bends the path too much and the satellite moves into a **smaller orbit**. Therefore, for a **stable orbit, the radius must change if the speed changes**. Satellites in **smaller orbits** feel stronger gravity and so travel **faster**; satellites in larger orbits move more slowly.

bullets: Circumference of a circle: **C = 2 x pi x r**.
Orbital speed: **v = 2 x pi x r / T** (m/s) where r is the orbital radius in m and T the period in s.
Rearranged: **T = 2 x pi x r / v** and **r = v x T / (2 x pi)**.
Radius is measured from the **centre** of the planet, so for a satellite above the surface use r = planet radius + height.
Unit conversions: 1 hour = 3600 s, 1 day = 86 400 s, 1 km = 1000 m.
**Worked check:** Earth orbit: r = 1.5 x 10^11 m, T = 1 year = 3.15 x 10^7 s, so v is about 3.0 x 10^4 m/s (30 km/s).
The Earth's average orbital speed is large, but we do not feel it because we move with the Earth.
core.h: Orbital speed, orbital period and circumference
core.p: The **orbital period** T is the **time for one complete orbit**. During one orbit, a satellite in a circular orbit of radius r travels a distance equal to the **circumference** of its orbit, which is 2 x pi x r. Since **speed = distance / time**, the orbital speed is **v = 2 x pi x r / T**. You use this together with the radius to calculate speeds, or rearrange it to find the period or radius. Always convert units into metres and seconds first.

bullets: The rocket must give the satellite both the correct **height** and the correct **speed** for that height.
A satellite at the correct speed for its radius **keeps going without engines**, because there is little air resistance in space.
Boosting speed moves a satellite to a **higher orbit**; slowing a satellite makes it fall to a **lower orbit**.
In low orbits there is a tiny amount of air resistance, so some satellites slowly lose speed and must be adjusted to stay up.
Spacecraft re-entering Earth's atmosphere are slowed so they leave orbit.
Different uses need different orbits, but all obey the same speed-radius rule.
core.h: How satellites are put into stable orbits
core.p: To place a satellite in a stable orbit, a rocket first lifts it to the required height and then gives it the **sideways speed** needed for that height. Once at that speed it can remain in orbit without further fuel, because gravity provides the force that curves its path. If a satellite needs a different orbit, its speed is changed, which changes its radius. Because the speed and the radius are linked, a satellite cannot simply stay at a chosen height at any speed.

bullets: **Planets**: nearly circular orbits around the Sun; their speeds are almost constant.
**Moons**: orbit planets, e.g. Earth's Moon takes about 27 days to orbit the Earth (about one month).
**Comets** (extension): elliptical orbits, with the Sun not at the centre; speed changes along the orbit.
In any orbit, gravity is the force that provides the acceleration.
A body nearer the central mass experiences **stronger gravity** and moves **faster**.
The larger the orbit, the longer the **orbital period**.
core.h: Orbits of planets, moons and comets
core.p: The planets orbit the Sun in **nearly circular** orbits, which is why the circular model works well for GCSE. The Moon orbits the Earth, and artificial satellites do too. **Comets** follow very stretched **elliptical** orbits that take them far from the Sun and then close to it. In an elliptical orbit the speed is not constant: the comet moves **faster when it is nearer the Sun** (where gravity is stronger) and **slower when it is further away**. This elliptical behaviour is an extension beyond the circular case studied at GCSE.

bullets: Step 1: **gravity** provides a force towards the centre of the orbit.
Step 2: the force is **perpendicular** to the velocity so it changes the direction, not the speed.
Step 3: velocity is a **vector**; its direction is changing so the velocity changes.
Step 4: a change in velocity means **acceleration**, even though speed is constant.
Step 5: for a stable orbit **speed and radius are linked**; a different speed means a different radius.
Step 6: smaller orbits have **faster speeds** and shorter periods.
core.p: Explanations of orbits follow a recognisable chain of reasoning. First state the force: gravity acts towards the centre. Next note the velocity is tangent to the orbit and so changes direction. Then say that a change of direction means a change of velocity, which means acceleration. Finally link speed and radius. If you can write this chain quickly, you can answer most questions.

bullets: Typical pattern: as **orbital radius increases, orbital period increases** and orbital speed decreases.
A graph of period against radius curves upward (period rises faster than radius).
Check units, convert to m and s, then use v = 2 x pi x r / T.
Round sensibly (2 or 3 significant figures) and always give the unit.
Estimate first: Earth's orbital speed about 30 km/s; a low Earth orbit satellite about 7.7 km/s.
Compare data sets by quoting figures from the table.
core.p: You may be given data for several planets or satellites showing orbital radius and period, and asked to describe a pattern. Planets further from the Sun have **longer periods** and lower orbital speeds. You may also have to calculate the speed from radius and period. When reading tables, check the units (km vs m, days vs seconds) before calculating.

bullets: **Forces (4.5):** gravity as a non-contact force; resultant force and acceleration.
**Motion:** velocity is a vector; acceleration is a change in velocity.
**Space physics (4.8):** the Solar system, stars and the Big Bang all depend on gravity.
**Maths skills:** circumference of a circle; rearranging equations; standard form.
**Energy:** a satellite moving at constant speed has constant kinetic energy in a circular orbit.
**Technology:** communications, weather and navigation depend on artificial satellites.
core.p: Orbital motion draws together several parts of GCSE physics. It uses ideas about forces and resultant force, speed, vectors and acceleration, and the gravitational field concept. It also supports the study of the Solar system and the life cycle of stars, because gravity is the force that forms stars and holds the Solar system together.

exam: **1-mark:** name the force that keeps a satellite in orbit: **gravity**. Name the difference between natural and artificial satellites.
**2-mark 'explain acceleration':** 'speed is constant but the **direction is changing**, so the **velocity is changing** and the object is **accelerating**'.
**2-mark 'direction of force':** 'towards the **centre** of the orbit'.
**3-mark 'explain orbit':** gravity acts towards centre, perpendicular to velocity, so changes direction without changing speed.
**Radius and speed:** 'for a stable orbit, if the speed changes the radius must change; smaller orbits mean greater speed'.
**Calculations:** v = 2 x pi x r / T; convert to m and s; check significant figures; give units.
**Radius trap:** measure radius from the centre of the planet; add the planet's radius to the height above the surface.
**Data questions:** describe the pattern with figures: as radius increases, period increases.
**Command words:** 'explain' needs a reason; 'describe' only the pattern; 'calculate' needs working.

mistakes.r: Velocity includes direction; direction changes in a circle, so velocity changes and the object accelerates.
mistakes.w: The satellite has constant velocity because its speed is constant.

mistakes.r: Gravity acts on it towards the centre of the orbit and provides the force needed for circular motion.
mistakes.w: There is no force on a satellite because it is in space.

mistakes.r: No forward force is needed; gravity acts at right angles to the motion and only changes direction.
mistakes.w: A force forwards keeps the satellite moving.

mistakes.r: Gravity is still strong; the satellite is continuously falling towards the planet while moving sideways.
mistakes.w: Satellites float because there is no gravity in space.

mistakes.r: For a stable orbit, if the speed changes the radius must change.
mistakes.w: A faster satellite stays in the same orbit.

mistakes.r: Satellites in smaller orbits move faster; those in larger orbits are slower.
mistakes.w: Satellites in higher orbits move faster.

mistakes.r: Gravity changes the direction, not the speed, in a circular orbit.
mistakes.w: Gravity speeds the satellite up in a circular orbit.

mistakes.r: Measure r from the centre of the planet, so add the planet radius to the height.
mistakes.w: Use of the planet surface as the orbital radius.

summary: AQA 4.8.1 (Physics only) asks you to explain that gravity provides the force that keeps planets, moons and satellites (natural and artificial) in orbit, why a body moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating because its velocity is changing, and why the radius of a stable orbit must change if the orbital speed changes. It matters because it links forces, speed and acceleration to real space applications.

terms.d: The curved path followed by an object moving around a star, planet or moon because of gravity.
An object that orbits a larger object in space.
A moon: a natural object that orbits a planet.
A man-made object put into orbit around a planet or moon.
An attractive non-contact force between objects with mass; it provides the force that keeps planets and satellites in orbit.
An orbit at constant distance from the body being orbited.
A vector quantity: the speed of an object in a given direction.
A scalar quantity: how fast an object moves, with no direction.
The rate of change of velocity; a change in direction counts as a change in velocity.
A quantity that has both size (magnitude) and direction.
A quantity that has size only.
The single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object.
The resultant force towards the centre of a circular path; in orbits it is provided by gravity.
An orbit in which the speed matches the radius so the satellite stays at a constant distance.
The time taken for one complete orbit.
The distance from the centre of the orbited body to the orbiting object.

worked.q: The Earth orbits the Sun at an average radius of 1.5 x 10^11 m. One orbit takes 3.15 x 10^7 s. Calculate the orbital speed of the Earth. (3 marks)
steps: Distance in one orbit = circumference = 2 x pi x r = 2 x 3.14 x 1.5 x 10^11 = 9.42 x 10^11 m.

worked.q: A satellite orbits the Earth at a height of 400 km above the surface. The radius of the Earth is 6370 km and the satellite takes 92 minutes for one orbit. Calculate its orbital speed. (4 marks)
steps: Circumference = 2 x pi x 6.77 x 10^6 = 4.25 x 10^7 m.

worked.ans: Although its speed is constant, the direction of the satellite is always changing, so its velocity is changing and it is therefore accelerating. The resultant force (gravity) acts towards the centre of the orbit.
worked.q: Explain why a satellite moving in a circular orbit at constant speed is accelerating. (3 marks)
steps: The direction of motion changes continuously, so velocity changes.
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, so the satellite accelerates towards the centre because of gravity.
